title: How the weight loss market is prompting pharma biggies to look at India afresh
description:
It is different this time, because of the burgeoning weight loss drugs market, whose buoyancy is making global pharma giants such as Lilly and Novo look at India afresh.
That is one box ticked with the India market getting fattened by weight loss drugs.
“We have competitors that are in the subcutaneous space also give 21 percent weight loss at the highest dose.
The Wegovy pill has been launched first in the US where it has an 85 percent share of the weight loss tablet market.
After weight loss Both Lilly and Novo are betting on differentiated therapies as they expand their India portfolios.
text:
Additionally, the India centre has developed new systems and processes that are shared with other centres and are being adopted globally. “In this, India is really a peer to our US and European centres, particularly for clinical trials,” says Ricks.

Fat is the fuel

Eli Lilly has been in India for more than three decades. Ricks says this is the company’s fourth or fifth push in the country. Earlier efforts—including a 1993 partnership with Ranbaxy, once India’s largest pharma company which eventually passed into the hands of Sun Pharma, and launches in areas such as oncology and antibiotics—failed to gain enough traction. Lilly did not have products to reach large sections of the population.

It is different this time, because of the burgeoning weight loss drugs market, whose buoyancy is making global pharma giants such as Lilly and Novo look at India afresh. It is no longer merely a large market for cheaper, generic versions of the drugs MNCs spend billions to develop, or a country where they delay introducing their new drugs for as long as possible and then bear in stoic silence the loss of revenue as generic versions rush in.

India is now also a hub of drug development for them and may become one of manufacturing as well. Lilly last year committed $1 billion to expand its contract manufacturing network here. Novo, the Danish pharma giant that competes with Lilly globally, shares its rival’s sentiments.

Advertise Your Brand →

Reach your target audience via high-impact campaigns, sponsored content and high-impact solutions.

“In the obesity space also, we have always had a very strong development presence in India,” Novo’s executive vice-president of R&D and chief scientific officer, Martin Hoist Lange, said in an interview with Forbes India in late September. “So, a good proportion of our clinical trials is with people from India. Thereby also obliging ourselves to launch our products in India and making our products available for people in India. So, from an R&D perspective, India is an integral part of how we do our development.”

Lilly is setting up a joint laboratory with an Indian partner, whose name it has not yet disclosed, focused on process development work. At the same time, it is working with Indian manufacturers to produce registered starting materials and other key ingredients used in some of its biggest products, including its weight loss blockbuster Mounjaro. The move is part of a broader effort to diversify supply chains.

“We have all become concerned that we were over relying on one country for these,” says Ricks. Establishing an Indian base for critical inputs, he adds, has become strategically important. About a year into the effort, “it is going really well”.

For now, Lilly’s manufacturing footprint in India remains export-oriented. But that could change as the demand grows. “We tend to locate our manufacturing plants near our largest markets. So far, India has not been a large market. But as India grows, we’ll need to produce more, and we can look at production close to the market here,” says Ricks.

Indeed, everyone likes to have their development and manufacturing bases as close to their largest markets as possible. That is one box ticked with the India market getting fattened by weight loss drugs. The other factor, the unexpected catalyst, is artificial intelligence, or AI, which is changing the mechanics of pharma research.

In a blog titled, ‘We Must Pace the Frontier’, Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei says: “I believe that AI could cure most major diseases in the next 5–10 years.”

Might of weight loss

In March 2025, Eli Lilly launched Mounjaro in India. By October, it had become the country’s top‑selling drug by value overtaking the long‑standing market leader, GSK’s Augmentin. In June 2025, Novo entered the fray with Wegovy, its obesity‑focused semaglutide injection, and launched the much-awaited Ozempic in India in December.

Both Ozempic and Mounjaro make you feel full sooner and for longer. But Mounjaro, which was approved five years after Ozempic and whose chemical name is tirzepatide, acts on both GLP-1 and GIP receptors. These are specialised proteins found on the surface of cells and play an important role in how the human body processes energy. Ozempic, whose chemical name is semaglutide, works only on GLP-1.

India’s weight loss drugs category is estimated to have risen to ₹2,300 crore from ₹750 crore a year prior, largely driven by semaglutide going off patent on March 20, 2026, which saw 23 Indian generic versions of it launched within 24 hours.

“It is inevitable,” says Ricks. “That is a by-product of our industry.” He however adds that the flood of generics has not affected Mounjaro’s growth. Instead, he says, “It has brought more people into the market.”

These would be people inclined towards weight loss drugs but daunted by their high prices. “This is part of the normal cycle of our business,” he says. The same thing happened in Brazil and Canada.

How does an inventor company convince buyers to pay more for their medicines despite the presence of cheaper generics?

“Starting mostly with the physicians...,” says Ricks. “Through physicians we communicate… The clinical trials we have conducted… That if they are given a choice, what is the best alternative for people with obesity, people with diabetes… Now we have cardiovascular data that shows heart protection… And point out those differences when they are recommending something to a patient. I think we have comprehensive evidence versus semaglutide that is pretty convincing to most trained doctors.”

Now everything in that market needs to be assessed all over again, because the next big thing is round the corner. The market that has so far been injectables is about to receive its first dose of pills.

Beyond the needle

Oral GLP-1 pills are expected to come to India in the first half of 2027.

“It is always helpful to be the first,” says Ricks. “But in the case of cardio metabolic health, it seems less important because these are chronic medications, and often the best one rises to the top. We saw that in the injectable market.”

With the pills coming into the market, the fear is they will cannibalise injectables. There are use cases for both. Pills work well for patients who don’t want to inject themselves and those who prefer lower prices. Clinical studies by Eli Lilly show that in order to maintain a certain weight over time, patients can either lower the dose of Mounjaro or switch to Foundayo, which is Lilly’s oral GLP-1.

The differentiation between Lilly and Novo’s products boils down to chemistry. Ricks says Mounjaro (tirzepatide) has achieved massive success partly because it mimics two hormones released by the gut after a meal, helping regulate appetite and blood sugar. Novo’s semaglutide, sold as Ozempic for type 2 diabetes and Wegovy for obesity, works as a GLP-1 receptor. “The basic biology works a similar way. We have a lot of respect for our competitor,” says Ricks.

Novo’s oral semaglutide is a peptide—a short chain of amino acids—which brings its own formulation challenges: Ensuring the drug survives digestion and is absorbed into the bloodstream.

Lilly took a different approach with orforglipron (Foundayo), using a small chemical compound rather than a chain of amino acids (peptides) to activate the GLP-1 receptor. Ricks says this approach was more challenging scientifically but made production easier to scale up.

Novo’s Lange did not reveal when his company’s weight loss pill will come to India, but emphasised that Wegovy was the only drug in the obesity space that had an established cardiovascular risk reduction, by 20 percent, and a liver risk reduction. “And those benefits are also seen with the Wegovy pill,” he said.

He highlighted his drug’s benefits over its rival’s. “We have competitors that are in the subcutaneous space also give 21 percent weight loss at the highest dose. They don’t have the cardiovascular and liver benefits. They have a small molecule GLP-1 as a tablet. But that only gives 12 percent weight loss,” said Lange.

The Wegovy pill has been launched first in the US where it has an 85 percent share of the weight loss tablet market. “And we are slowly but surely launching outside of the US. So far, we have launched in three countries outside of the US, with the next being Mexico,” he said.

After weight loss

Both Lilly and Novo are betting on differentiated therapies as they expand their India portfolios.

Beyond weight loss drugs, Lilly plans to bring medicines to India across therapies. But for that it must grapple with standards that are not the same as the international benchmarks for registration, including local data and local clinical trials. “Doing clinical trials in India is more complicated than other markets. So, we are working with the government to streamline that,” says Ricks.

Dementia currently affects 8.8 million people in India, and it is expected to inflict 16.9 million by 2036. In May 2026, Eli Lilly launched its Alzheimer’s drug Kisunla (donanemab), also known as Lormalzi in India. It costs ₹91,688 for a 350-mg vial, which needs to be taken as an intravenous infusion once every four weeks.

This, in a price sensitive market, is expensive, made even more so by the wafer-thin health insurance coverage in the country which translates into patients paying out of their own pockets. Lilly says all its medicines are priced as per the GDP per capita of a country. “While Kisunla and Mounjaro may still seem expensive relative to their generic alternatives, there is a pretty big discount relative to the European or US pricing,” says Ricks. “That’s how we fund our research and development.”

Novo is excited about a new molecule called setagantide, which during Phase II trials showed 24 percent weight loss in 36 weeks and is now in Phase III. However, it too is awake to other opportunities in India. “From a commercial perspective, we intend to launch our products in India. It goes beyond obesity. In India, we are in diabetes, blood disorders, haemophilia, and sickle cell disease,” said Lange.

AI-Powered R&D

Amodei’s blog might suggest that the next breakthrough cancer medicine is a prompt away. “That,” Ricks says, “is not the case.”

Medicines live in the physical world. Innovator companies make a molecule that does not exist—a new chemical structure to interfere with biology. And it has to be safe. To prove a medicine’s efficacy and safety, it needs to be tested in people who have the disease. According to Ricks, there might only be a handful of medicines that can claim to be invented by AI and are in the human testing phase.

Lilly is deeply invested in AI for research and development, but in a different way.

Making early-stage drug research more efficient is one. Drawing on data from past laboratory experiments, Lilly’s models predict how a molecule might behave, how long it could remain active in the bloodstream, or whether it might cause unwanted effects. These predictions help scientists avoid spending time on candidates likely to fail, speeding up research and reducing costs.

In September 2025, the company launched Lilly TuneLab. It is a collaborative artificial intelligence and machine learning drug discovery platform. This gives smaller biotech companies free access to AI tools that can help them identify promising drug candidates.

Separately, Lilly has invested $1 billion with NVIDIA to build the largest biologic supercomputer in the world, called LillyPod. It is training AI models to predict human biology and eventually generate ideas for new drug programmes to help supercharge drug discovery. “It will take years to fully train models useful to scientists,” says Ricks.

Novo, in April, announced a partnership with OpenAI and in September it partnered with Anthropic. Both the partnerships are to embed advanced artificial intelligence across its entire drug development and operational pipeline.

“AI helps to amplify the volume and the speed, but it also helps by providing more insights and analysing the data that we generate. In the clinical space, it is also a huge productivity gain,” says Lange. Though AI can amplify and enable research, it cannot work in isolation. “We still need the human insights on top or in parallel with what we do with AI,” he adds.

name: Best Buy
title: Best Buy opens Canada's first 'Best Buy Business Centres' in the GTA - Toronto Star
description: Markham and Mississauga are the first of a new ‘store within a store,’ catering to small to medium businesses.
text:
Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) account for an incredible
98 per cent
of all employer businesses in Canada.
No wonder this critical workforce — typically defined as organizations with fewer than 500 employees — is considered the backbone of our country’s economy. As such, these companies often rely on tech to remain lean, nimble, and competitive in a fast-changing business environment.
Starting with two locations in the GTA,
Best Buy Canada
is aiming to arm SMEs with the latest gear in a first-of-its-kind, “store-within-a-store” space.
Called Best Buy Business Centres, these dedicated areas are designed for small-to-medium businesses to discover, demo, and buy business grade technology with expert support.
“We see a need in the Canadian market,” said Christian Leadbeater, vice president of Best Buy Business at Best Buy Canada. “Enterprises have large resellers, managed service providers and manufacturers working with them directly, while small and mid-sized businesses are often left to figure things out on their own.”
Leadbeater said that these businesses need a partner who can help them understand which products and services fit. “A physical space lets them see, test, and talk it through with an expert before they commit. We already have the store footprint, so a store within a store is the fastest way to deliver that.”
Contributed
Customers can meet one-on-one with a Best Buy Business advisor or account manager and get their hands on commercial-grade technology that isn’t available in Best Buy Canada’s regular stores.
Business customers can seek assistance with planning, procurement, and deployment, whether that be for one location or sites across the country. Products made available in these business centres are supported by Geek Squad, with services range from AV installation to device lifecycle management.
Each centre includes interactive demo spaces and business-grade devices from brands such as Apple, HP, Lenovo, Jabra, Square and Xerox, among others.
ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
Some solutions showcased are digital signage and content management, interactive displays, business laptops, printers, and headsets, as well as networking, conference room technologies, and more, allowing businesses to make confident decisions and deploy quickly.
Launching ‘Best Buy Businesses Centres’
Markham, Ont. opens first, with a grand opening on October 15 (
5000 Hwy 7 East
), followed by Heartland Mississauga (
6075 Mavis Road
)  in November.
“These first two locations are a pilot and the first of their kind in Canada,” shared Leadbeater. “We’ll learn a lot from how businesses use these spaces, and the pilot lays the foundation for the potential for many more centres across the country.”
Contributed
Best Buy Business Centres are open to businesses of all sizes, as well as non-profits, public sector organizations, and schools. This includes healthcare and fitness; professional services, such as law, insurance, accounting and real estate offices; hospitality, restaurants and retail; trades, construction, and manufacturing; creative and production agencies; and daycare facilities, public and private schools, and colleges and universities, to name just a few industries.
Leadbeater says businesses either book an appointment with a Best Buy Business advisor ahead of time, or simply walk in.
Why a ‘store-within-a-store’
Businesses customers already shop at Best Buy Canada, maintained Leadbeater, and so it made sense to build a new and dedicated SME experience in a place shoppers were already familiar with.
“In fact, we see that business customers shop more often than retail consumers, both in store and online. Many of our products in store work as well for the office environment as they do in the home [but] there are so many other products and solutions that businesses should see and experience,” Leadbeater explained.
“What many haven’t had is an experience built around business-grade technology and business needs. Businesses are technology driven and having a place to truly experience that technology is a great benefit,” he added.

title: L'Oréal's Top Premium Brand Enters the Cutthroat Hair & Body Care Market Competition
description:
In fact, it is not only these two high-end brands, but also brands such as Pantene and Off&Relax, the hair care brand under Proya, that are continuously deploying the high-end hair care track.
Sourced from Clarins official website Qingyan noticed that the "Precious Luxury Care" hair care product line that recently completed the filing of imported cosmetics in China is exactly this "Hair Therapy" series.
There are two types of core players coexisting in the current international high-end hair care market: one is professional hair care brands that deeply cultivate the salon channel, and the other is top skincare brands that cross-border into the hair care sector.
According to Qingyan Intelligence's "2026 Hair Care and Hairdressing Market Insight Report" (hereinafter referred to as "2026 Hair Care Market Report"), in the first half of 2026, the size of the hair care and hairdressing market grew to 46.4 billion yuan, with a year-on-year growth rate of 7.97%.
According to Qingyan Intelligence's "2026 Hair Care Market Report", Off&Relax is the top-ranked domestic brand among the TOP20 hair care brands on Taobao/Tmall in the first half of 2026.
text:
Recently, Qingyan noticed that Clarins and La Maison de Beauté Carita, the ultra-luxury skincare brand under L'Oréal, have completed the filing of multiple hair care products in China, marking the first time both brands have officially introduced their hair care lines to the Chinese market.

An interesting detail is that the filing time of the two major brands' hair care products is almost synchronized. In fact, it is not only these two high-end brands, but also brands such as Pantene and Off&Relax, the hair care brand under Proya, that are continuously deploying the high-end hair care track. The high-end hair care sector has already seen fierce competition across the board.

International Giants Bring Skincare Ingredients "To The Scalp"

From a global market perspective, Clarins' layout in hair care is not new, but this is the brand's first complete hair and scalp care line.

In July this year, Clarins officially announced the launch of a brand new hair care line named "Hair Therapy", which focuses on the long-term health management of scalp and hair strands with "skincare-level formulation philosophy".

It is worth mentioning that Clarins has already made layouts in the hair care category before, and once entered the Chinese market, which can be traced back to the men's series Vitality Shampoo that completed the filing in 2009. However, this "Hair Therapy" line is defined by the group as "the first complete hair and scalp care series", which builds a complete hair care system with 5 core products.

It is understood that the core proposition of the "Hair Therapy" line launched by Clarins this time is "the scalp itself is a complete piece of skin". Relying on the R&D laboratory that shares the same origin with facial skincare, this line develops exclusive F_03 technology, compounding two plant active ingredients, organic white iris extract and saffron flower polyphenols, to help promote hair renewal, and creates a total of 5 products including strengthening scalp serum, shampoo, conditioner, hair mask and hair care oil.

Sourced from Clarins official website

Qingyan noticed that the "Precious Luxury Care" hair care product line that recently completed the filing of imported cosmetics in China is exactly this "Hair Therapy" series. Except for the hair mask that has not been filed, the remaining 4 products have all completed the filing.

Sourced from the imported ordinary cosmetics filing platform of the National Medical Products Administration

In addition, Qingyan's sorting found that there are far more international brands than just Clarins that migrate skincare ingredients/technologies to the high-end hair care track.

There are two types of core players coexisting in the current international high-end hair care market: one is professional hair care brands that deeply cultivate the salon channel, and the other is top skincare brands that cross-border into the hair care sector. The former builds professional trust endorsement relying on salon genes, while the latter directly reuses skincare laboratories, core active ingredients and technical patents, and the two forces jointly raise the value ceiling of high-end hair care.

Guerlain follows a similar path to Clarins. In June this year, multiple hair care products of Guerlain's Abeille Royale series completed domestic filing. This series is derived from its signature Abeille Royale skincare line, extending the accumulated "black bee honey repair technology" in the skincare line to the scalp and hair strands, with product lines covering hair care serum, repair hair mask, conditioner, shampoo and other products, and the price of each product is above 750 yuan.

Sourced from Guerlain official website

In addition, SENSAI under Kao and South Korean skincare brand Medicube also enter the scalp care sector with skincare technologies, with prices concentrated in the range of 200 to 750 yuan.

This group of long-established players in the skincare field and new entrants in the hair care track all output the skincare research results that the brands have accumulated for a long time, to support the high value sense of their products. Among many international groups, L'Oréal is a player with a very comprehensive layout in the high-end hair care track.

Data from Global Market Insights shows that L'Oréal Group accounts for about 24.9% of the global high-end hair care market in 2025. It is understood that L'Oréal Professional Products Division has a total of 10 brands, spanning high-end lines such as Kérastase and Shu Uemura Art of Hair, as well as mass salon lines such as L'Oréal Paris Hair Care and Matrix.

Among them, Kérastase is positioned by L'Oréal as the "absolute core" of the professional hair care sector. As the second largest market of Kérastase in the world, China has long seen the brand rank firmly at the top of the hair care category on mainstream domestic e-commerce platforms, forming an overwhelming leading position in the high-end hair care track. In China, on the one hand, Kérastase taps into segmented opportunities with new products such as "Hairline Mask", on the other hand, it stabilizes its user base and repurchase base with classic best-selling items such as "Camellia Hair Care Oil".

In addition, to further supplement the incremental growth of the track, L'Oréal acquired the high-end professional hair care brand COLOR WOW in 2025. This brand is characterized by a small number of SKUs and strong visual effects, priced in the range of 200-300 yuan, filling the gap between the positioning below Kérastase and above mass brands.

At present, COLOR WOW Tmall Global Flagship Store has put 4 products on the shelves (one product has multiple links), which are smoothing spray, cleansing spray, polishing hair mask and shampoo. Among them, the smoothing spray has topped the Tmall repair hair care spray positive review list.

COLOR WOW product material picture

Not only that, Qingyan also noticed that Carita, the luxury skincare brand under L'Oréal, also completed the filing of the "Carita Brightening & Moisturizing" hair care series in June 2026. The products include shampoo, hair mask and hair care oil, which have not been officially put on the shelves in official channels for the time being.

Sourced from the Cosmetics Supervision APP

It is understood that Carita is called by L'Oréal "the most luxurious skincare brand of the group". It started as a hair salon in 1945, and in the following decades, it continued to lead the development of the skincare industry through innovations in exfoliating products, injection products and beauty devices.

Sourced from L'Oréal official website and Carita Tmall Flagship Store

The "Brightening & Moisturizing" hair care series launched this year is the first independent product line specially targeted at the hair care market launched by Carita after returning to the high-end hair care sector.

Recently, Carita has released multiple brand history contents on social media platforms, starting to strengthen its own origin gene in hair care. For example, the founding sisters of the brand once left a sentence: "Hair is an exclamation mark on the silhouette." In their view, hairstyle is never just a decoration, it changes a woman's silhouette, and also changes the way she is seen. This may also be the preparation made by Carita for the landing of its hair care series in the Chinese market.

Interestingly, the filing time of Carita's hair care products basically coincides with the filing window of new hair care products of Guerlain and Clarins, which indirectly confirms the industry trend that top skincare brands are betting on the hair care sector.

Generally speaking, migrating the skincare system to the hair care track has become a common practice for leading international brands to deploy the high-end market. Brands begin to create hair care products with skincare R&D standards and formulation logic, and consumers have gradually developed the consumption habit of evaluating scalp and hair care products with the evaluation criteria for skincare products.

Avoiding the Home Turf of Big Brands, Domestic Brands Achieve High-end Growth Through Scientific Research Segmentation

text:
Andrea Orcel-led Italian banking giant UniCredit has sought EU antitrust approval for its takeover of the German bank Commerzbank, with regulators setting a November 16 deadline for their decision, according to a European Commission filing on Friday.

UniCredit’s two-year pursuit of acquiring Commerzbank, which faced intense opposition from the German lender and government, ultimately succeeded in July 2026, with Commerzbank entering into M&A talks with its Italian counterpart.

UniCredit, as of now, holds a total stake of 47.59% in Commerzbank (approximately 47.6%), which translates to 49.65% of the voting rights once treasury shares are cancelled.

European regulators, from their part, are backing cross-border mergers to create European banking champions.

The Commission, which is the EU competition enforcer, has two options as of now: either clear the deal with or ⁠without concessions during its preliminary review, or open a full-scale ⁠investigation if it has serious concerns.

Orcel, looking to take control of his acquisition target, is also eyeing the overhaul of the German lender’s supervisory board by as early ‌as January 2027.

As per the reports of the Financial Times, the Italian lender plans to call an extraordinary general meeting once it receives the remaining regulatory approvals needed to take control of Germany’s second-largest bank.

“UniCredit expects to secure control by the end of February and replace all 10 shareholder representatives on Commerzbank’s 20-member supervisory board, giving it an effective majority,” the media outlet stated in September.

While Berlin has softened its stance on a potential deal after UniCredit built a stake of nearly 50% in the German lender, Friedrich Merz has continued to demand that Commerzbank remain listed, keep its ⁠Frankfurt headquarters, and maintain its role in financing German medium-sized companies at home and abroad.

Germany won the right to appoint two board members ⁠when it rescued Commerzbank in 2009 during the global financial crisis. It retains a stake of 13.3% in the bank.

As per reports, Orcel wants sweeping changes at Commerzbank, including the departures of CEO Bettina Orlopp and Chairman Jens Weidmann.

Orlopp has, however, maintained a cooperative stance, proposing that Commerzbank could potentially acquire UniCredit’s German bank HVB in shares to create a mutually beneficial merger.

Orlopp, speaking at a financial conference during September, ⁠said such a deal structure was one of several “options on the table” as a way to increase UniCredit’s shareholding in Commerzbank.

Orlopp also said that the other ways to structure a deal include a ⁠simple merger between Commerzbank and UniCredit or by UniCredit making another offer to the remaining ⁠Commerzbank shareholders—”most likely with a premium”—to get its shareholding ⁠above 90%.

She concluded by stating that all three basic options are available.

text:
By Jacqueline Munis

Among Americans’ many concerns about data centers—from the constant humming sound to high electricity prices—heavy water consumption stands out. Residents of towns with data centers have reported contaminated water, low water pressure, and unauthorized siphoning, putting one of life’s essentials under threat.

Nvidia thinks it has the solution for that: its new server infrastructure.

The company announced on Monday that its newest AI servers will entirely use liquid cooling, a method that eliminates the need for air-cooling fans that rely on water.

Instead, heat will be dissipated by a liquid coolant made of water and propylene glycol that’s recirculated in a closed loop. The company says the system doesn’t need to draw in new water.

“We have eliminated massive amounts of power usage and pretty much all water usage,” Ali Heydari, Nvidia’s director of data center cooling and infrastructure, said in a statement.

In addition, the coolant can remain operational at temperatures of up to 45 °C or 113 °F, a much higher temperature than previous systems.

The move towards a more energy-efficient system comes as the United Nations predicted earlier this month that AI-related water consumption could equal the annual needs of 1.3 billion people by the end of the decade.

Meanwhile, Nvidia is not the only company working towards significantly reducing its water consumption. In August 2024, Microsoft announced that its new data centers will stop using water for cooling, saving more than 125 million liters of water per year per data center.

“The thing that’s exciting about what Nvidia announced is it shows really what’s possible in terms of pushing up this liquid input temperature to 45°C,” said Andrew A. Chien, a professor of computer science at the University of Chicago. “It’s super important to push it up, because in many cases it allows you to do that cooling, that exhausting of heat to the outside environment without running HVAC units, without running air conditioners. Because if it’s cool enough outside, you don’t need to.”

Chien directs the CERES Center for Unstoppable Computing. For the past 10 years, the center has studied how to make data centers more efficient and reduce their negative environmental impacts. A higher cooling temperature goes against conventional wisdom, he explained. The industry standard is 30°C, which requires much more air conditioning to maintain.

“The reason that they want to do this is that if you can cool the chips at a higher temperature, it becomes easier to vent that heat into the outside environment, because it’s a higher temperature supply, and heat flows downhill,” Chien said.

While he said zero water use is unrealistic, liquid cooling will significantly reduce the need for water. The catch is that these systems are expensive.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment on the costs of the systems or if the company will be retrofitting existing data centers with the technology.

The company estimates that a 50-megawatt hyperscale facility could save over $4 million a year in cooling-related energy and water costs by moving to liquid-cooled infrastructure.

“It is a direction that more people should be trying to get to, because it’ll reduce the total power consumption of these large data centers,” Chien said.

text:
This post was created in partnership with Best Buy Ads

Key takeaways

CTV turns passive watching into an interactive experience that brands can leverage.

Compared to linear TV, brands can react to cultural moments and respond faster with CTV ads.

The TV remote control lets viewers interact with ads, giving marketers unique data points and targeting capabilities.

Could CTV take a page from social and reinvent the legacy television ad-watching experience?

During an ADWEEK House Advertising HQ group chat co-hosted with Best Buy Ads, marketing leaders discussed how commerce-powered CTV is poised to reshape what was once passive consumer television-watching into a highly targeted, interactive experience that drives business outcomes for brands.

A new frontier in television-led shopping

Patrick Albano, chief revenue officer for Best Buy Ads, kicked off the discussion on connected TV with a bold statement.

“What you’re seeing now is actual sales information, actual consumer graphs that show what people like and what they might buy, and then applying that to television,” he said. “I think the things we’re talking about are really going to revolutionize the way people watch TV.”

Catherine Fanone, senior sales director at LG Ad Solutions, shared that her company partners with Best Buy Ads to connect TV storytelling with a deeper understanding of shopper and brand outcomes.

“Best Buy Ads bring the commerce intelligence while LG brings the scale, the attention, and a more advanced screen environment. Hopefully, we can help brands really understand more how television connects or contributes to the path to purchase,” Fanone said.

The final part of the equation is reaching consumers in new, innovative ways.

“It was really hard to be culturally relevant on TV previously because you had to think so far in advance for when this is going to air, and you couldn’t be reactive to something that’s happening in real time,” explained Ty Stafford, founder and CEO of Hello Party.

Now, brands can do that on TV just like they do on social, he added. “You can make something that’s polished and looks good and happens to also be culturally relevant. And very few people are taking advantage of that right now.”

The two-way power of the remote

Albano pointed out that in a vertical like consumer electronics, buying happens in refresh cycles (e.g., buying a new phone every two or three years, or a TV or laptop every five to seven years). Data and insights can help brands understand where a specific customer is on that journey so they can get the right messaging to that person.

“Who’s five or seven years away from purchase? Maybe that’s the branding audience. Or who’s a week away, and maybe that’s your sales audience,” Albano explained. “The onus is on us to help provide that data and make it palatable. But that’s never been available for TV advertising before.”

One important tool helping drive some of these insights is the remote control, explained Rob Aksman, president and co-founder of BrightLine.

“Now that TV can be interacted with using the remote control, there are additional data signals that never existed before,” Aksman shared. Unlike traditional TV that relies on Nielsen ratings to determine how many viewers saw something, now there are signals coming in with every single click of the remote, he continued.

Brands are theoretically able to track every click or interaction. “All of those data signals can just feed this brain and this engine for better targeting and knowing when to follow up,” said Aksman.

Ending repeated commercial overkill

Aksman and the other panelists touched on the frustration of seeing the same ad over and over during an hours-long streaming binge.

“Every commercial is just saying ‘hello, nice to meet you,’ as if you haven’t seen it 10 times before,” said Aksman. He hopes more brands start taking advantage of new capabilities that allow them to sequence creative and use multiple, personalized, and engaging versions where data informs the next ad. “All of that is possible now. It’s just a matter of upstreaming it and making it happen,” he said.

Best of all, added Miles Fisher, VP of global strategic advertising partnerships at Roku, it’s not only large legacy brands that can do this.

“There’s this awesome opportunity for growth marketers and small and medium-sized brands to actually win the attention economy on streaming and CTV with these interactive ads, performance and outcomes,” Fisher said. “As streaming gets more democratized, CPMs are becoming more approachable to brands.”

text:
Delta Air Lines, Inc. (NYSE:DAL) has cut its 2026 earnings forecast despite reporting record third-quarter revenue, as surging jet fuel prices continue to overwhelm strong travel demand and higher ticket prices. On October 9, the airline reduced its adjusted EPS guidance to $5.10-$5.60 from $6.50-$7.50, citing an expected $6 billion increase in annual fuel expenses. The revision highlights a difficult investment question: how much of Delta's premium revenue growth can translate into sustainable earnings while one of its largest operating costs remains elevated?

Third-quarter adjusted revenue increased 15.7% to approximately $17.6 billion, but adjusted EPS of $1.72 missed consensus expectations. Fuel expenses rose 62% to $4.1 billion, exceeding management's July forecast by more than $500 million, while adjusted operating margin declined to 9.4% from 11.1%. The results demonstrate that even substantial revenue growth cannot guarantee margin expansion when fuel costs increase faster than an airline's ability to recover them through pricing.

The stock has gained over 20% during the last 6-months, compared to a 33.88% gain for Insider Monkey Billionaire Index and +18.18% return for State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust.

Pixabay/Public Domain

Premium Revenue Is Providing Support, But Fuel Remains the Bigger Driver

Delta Air Lines, Inc. (NYSE:DAL) continues to benefit from its emphasis on premium travelers and loyalty-related revenue. Premium revenue increased 18% year-over-year in Q3, while loyalty-related revenue also grew 18%. Remuneration from its American Express partnership increased 15% and remains on track to exceed $9 billion for the year, providing an additional revenue stream beyond conventional passenger ticket sales.

However, the company's ability to offset fuel inflation remains limited. Delta Air Lines, Inc. (NYSE:DAL) expects jet fuel to average approximately $4.25 per gallon in Q4, compared with $3.61 in Q3, and management has acknowledged that prices could remain elevated for some time. Although the airline has benefited from higher fares and disciplined capacity growth, additional price increases could eventually weaken passenger demand, particularly among more price-sensitive travelers.

Delta's Monroe refinery near Philadelphia provides some protection, with management expecting more than $700 million in benefits during 2026. The facility allows the company to retain refining profits that can partially offset higher fuel costs, particularly when the spread between crude oil and refined products widens. Nevertheless, that benefit remains relatively small compared with the projected $6 billion annual fuel-cost increase, leaving operating profitability heavily exposed to energy prices.

The Valuation Depends on a Recovery in Unit Economics

Delta Air Lines, Inc. (NYSE:DAL) trades at approximately 15 times estimated 2026 earnings, a relatively modest multiple considering its premium customer base and diversified revenue streams. However, this valuation depends on the company's ability to recover margins despite elevated fuel costs. Consensus estimates anticipate a 6.36% EPS decline in 2026 before growth rebounds to 39.62% in 2027 and 30.62% in 2028. Its estimated P/E consequently falls from 15.07 times 2026 earnings to 8.26 times 2028 earnings, indicating that the apparent valuation discount depends heavily on the expected profitability recovery. The reduction in free cash flow guidance reinforces that uncertainty. Delta now expects approximately $2.5 billion in 2026 free cash flow, down from its previous $3 billion-$4 billion outlook, even as management continues targeting stronger long-term margins and balance-sheet improvement. Raymond James, Susquehanna, Bernstein, and Wells Fargo maintained positive ratings while adjusting their price targets ahead of earnings, reflecting confidence in underlying demand but concern about the duration of fuel-related pressure.

The revised outlook makes cash conversion an increasingly important consideration for investors, particularly given the gap between reported profitability and the cash available after capital expenditures. We previously examined whether Delta's cash flow is keeping pace with its earnings, a question that has become even more relevant following the airline's latest guidance reduction.

Institutional positioning has remained relatively constructive, with hedge-fund ownership increasing from 68 to 75 funds in Q2. Berkshire Hathaway increased its position by 44% to approximately 57.3 million shares, suggesting that some investors continued to favor Delta's longer-term earnings potential despite near-term industry headwinds.

The next test is whether Delta Air Lines, Inc. (NYSE:DAL) can sustain improvements in revenue per available seat mile while controlling nonfuel unit costs and preserving cash generation. Its premium offerings and refinery provide meaningful competitive advantages, but neither eliminates the industry's exposure to fuel volatility. At approximately 15 times estimated 2026 earnings, the stock could become attractive if fuel prices stabilize and operating margins recover. If elevated fuel costs persist, however, the earnings rebound embedded in consensus estimates may prove more difficult to achieve.

While we acknowledge the potential of DAL as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. text:
Microsoft is amping up its AI chip game.

On Monday, the company announced plans to expand its Azure Maia AI chip program to multi-gigawatt-scale deployments starting next year. Microsoft also said its next-generation Maia 300 chip will deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based competitors and will begin production deployments in 2027.

Microsoft is a giant hyperscaler and one of the world’s largest buyers of semiconductors and AI servers.

Key Context recently spoke with Scott Guthrie, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Cloud and AI, about the insatiable demand for AI infrastructure, the new Maia 300 AI chip, CPU demand and the current frontier AI model price war.

Perhaps no one understands what is happening in the AI industry today better than Guthrie. When I last interviewed him at Barron’s about a year ago, he was remarkably prescient about the explosive infrastructure buildout to come and the rise of agentic AI.

I fully expect that a year from now, we will look back on this conversation the same way, particularly his comments on AI cybersecurity trends and the rising demand for various components. I highly recommend reading the whole interview.

Here are lightly edited highlights from our conversation. I bolded the remarks I found most important:

Tae: What is the significance of the Maia 300 announcement?

Scott: We’re super excited about Maia 300 and the Maia program overall.

Stepping back, I think the key thing we’re trying to do as a company is how to be multi model. We’re supporting multiple models, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and our own first-party models. We have infrastructure around the world, including in all the countries that need sovereignty. There are more countries than ever in the world that want that.

We want to both embed the models in our applications and solutions. Enable customers to build their own applications with them, and then you know have a common, consistent security and compliance control plane, and really provide that trust that customers expect, which is their data is their data. They can build applications safely. They can deploy this AI safely and with sovereignty.

Ultimately, we want to make sure we have the capacity. And then importantly, the tokens per dollar from a TCO perspective to be leading price performance, and from an overall ROI perspective.

That’s where the silicon program in Maia comes into play because the more we can drive down the cost of inference, the more we can pass on savings to our customers. The more throughput we can get per watt, then ultimately the more capacity that we can deliver as well.

We have Maia 200 in production today. We’re super excited because we finished the tape out, and are announcing Maia 300, which is the next major evolution. That’ll start to go into broad scale deployment next year. Maia 300 is really when we’re expanding the program in a big, big way.

We do healthy volumes on Maia 200, but Maia 300 is when we will take it up a level. We will use it for our first-party offerings, which we’re already using with Maia 200. But then also for third-party with Foundry and our API service. An awful lot of people that are using the APIs from us and will ultimately be using Maia chips under the covers, benefiting both from the performance as well as the improved ROI and TCO benefits that it provides.

Tae: Is multi-gigawatt for next year, or is that broader over several years?

Starting next year. I think for Maia 300 in particular, we’re going to start deploying it next year. It’ll be a ramp. So I don’t know the exact time frame for when we’ll get to multi gigawatt. But basically from a supply chain perspective, we’re ordering a lot of Maia 300 chips. The supply chain is going to be seeing this in earnest, which is partly why we felt comfortable sharing the number.

And then, Maia 400 will come after 300, and 500 will be coming after 400. This is an ongoing program.

Tae: How do you think about using the different AI chips? Obviously, Microsoft is a big buyer of NVIDIA chips. AMD is in the picture. Is it whatever the customer asks for?

Yeah, we’re big partners of NVIDIA and AMD, and we’ll continue to be big partners of them. We’ve had great success with them and that partnership is multifaceted on many different elements.

Similarly, we’ve had a great partnership with Intel and AMD on the CPU side. Cobalt is our equivalent. CPUs, I would say are even a year ahead. We’re starting the ramp this year on Cobalt in a big way and getting to hundreds of millions of cores with Cobalt. But we’re still going to buy a bunch of AMD and Intel CPUs as well.

The same is going to be true for Nvidia and AMD. Even with OpenAI, we do partner with them on their own first party silicon program. We are trying to make sure that we are big tent in the same way that we’re multi model, we are multi silicon.

But we think there are unique things that we can do with our first-party silicon both from a capability perspective and in particular from a cost perspective that gives us some good advantages. It’s one of the reasons why we’re going so big with Maia.

Tae: There is a lot of debate about chip architecture between disaggregation and more flexible generalized chips. Where does Maia fit in? What were the tradeoffs that were made?

Well, from a Maia perspective, we are using AI heavily to build Maia. We’re big believers, obviously, in AI to build things. And then we really optimized Maia for large language model AI.

I think there we’ve seen, if you look at the latest models and the reasoning models, a heavy memory footprint. They use a lot of memory and the throughput is often one of the limiters. So it’s not just how much memory you have, but the aggregate throughput per second to memory makes an enormous difference in terms of the overall performance and subsequent TCO.

Because if you’re stalled on throughput, your tokens per dollar goes down, and if you have a tremendous amount of throughput, it goes up. And that’s one of the reasons why in the press release you might have noticed we quoted some of the statistics in terms of terabytes per second of memory bandwidth and the amount of memory that we have in terms of latest HBM. Both of those are part of the contributors for why we have such great performance and TCO with Maia, and are one of the key differentiators for it versus others in the market.

Similarly, the network and the scale up is another area that we’re going big on with Maia that we are finding really helps with large models.

And the Maia silicon instruction set is fairly generalized, so it can be used for both prefill and decode. And it supports a broader set of scenarios than say a TPU, as an example, and is not tied to any single model. We already have both OpenAI models as well as our Microsoft AI models running natively on top of it.

Tae: I noticed in the blog post you said less data movement is a critical part of the improvements. Can you expand upon that?

I think from an architecture perspective. The extent that you don’t need to move data between nodes, and instead you can get more density in a single place and do more computation on top of that. That does translate directly in terms of improvements on tokens per dollar, and then rough raw token throughput period.

If you look at the memory capabilities, both in terms of total amount, but then especially the throughput between the compute and the memory. And then also the scale up networking specs. I think those are probably two of the biggest areas where we’ve been able to minimize data movement and ultimately directly improve raw throughput and TCO.

Tae: What are you seeing in the CPU space? Demand for CPU seems to be taking off because of agentic AI. How are you managing that?

We’re seeing certainly with the agentic and long running agents in particular, we’re seeing a huge rise in terms of the need for CPUs. You’re also going to see from a security sandboxing perspective, a need for quickly spinning up and spinning down workloads on top of CPUs.

And so we’re investing very heavily, not just with Cobalt in general, but from an architecture perspective, how do we get to sub-second hypervisor-based VM activation teardown, so that you can actually have a very secure perimeter around the agents that’s hypervisor-based. As the models get richer, you’re going to really want to have VM level isolation around that workload that’s protected by a hypervisor with a very small API footprint surface area. The speed to create and tear those down is going to matter and how close can you can get them to the silicon is also going to matter.

Similarly, we’re seeing a tremendous amount of demand for storage. I think you’re going to see hard drives and SSDs be in short supply over the next couple years because these agentic workloads love data, they love storage, they love to be able to create data, and you know more and more is going to be logged in terms of prompts and outputs and so forth. And so, I think you’re going to see an insatiable demand for storage and compute and GPUs, all of which need data centers and power.

It is very much an end-to-end infrastructure problem, and we’re trying to design really the end-to-end system to do that. And so, with Azure obviously being the software control plane fabric that kind of orchestrates it all, and then within our hardware programs, we do have distinct teams for Cobalt and Maia, but they’re part of the same broader hardware team. And on the supply chain team, we have one supply chain team for all of our server components, and that is allowing us to get synergies across our organization and across the design, so that we really build it as one integrated system.

Tae: One year ago, you predicted there’s this wave of AI infrastructure demand and the supply demand imbalance where demand was much higher than supply. What’s your outlook over the next year? What you’re seeing in the AI infrastructure and Azure pipeline?

Yeah, it’s still, we’re definitely seeing a lot. We continue to see that that growth. So from that perspective, I don’t think there’s really been any change, other than you know a year later we have a lot more in the denominator already.

But from an overall growth perspective, I think the world still has a fairly insatiable demand for more capabilities. And I think a big change is the models have gotten a lot better in the last 12 months.

When you have reasoning models that can complete more tasks autonomously or complete more end-to-end tasks. You also find if you need to have a human approve something twelve steps of the way. You’re then gated on the humans to do stuff.

To the extent the model can do all those twelve steps and then show the finished result, you know you can do a lot more, and more importantly, you get a lot better return on investment if you’re automating a specific task or a business process. And that, in turn, with Jevons paradox creates yet more demand.

Because if the return is that much better for automating things, you tend to automate more. And so, I do think we’re also finding that as the intelligence gets better, the business outcomes get stronger, the demand increases.

Tae: What is going to happen over the next six to twelve months from the AI model and AI model vendor side? Give us a flavor of how you expect the capabilities to advance?

Today everyone would say if you look at engineering and coding, clearly AI has broken through, and pretty much every organization is looking to leverage AI for coding and for engineering. And people sort of just assume it’s a given from a productivity perspective.

You’ll see in the next few months ahead, the same is true for security and cyber security. I think every organization is either using AI today for security or will be shortly. As more bad actors use AI, the only way to defend against that will be actually to use AI more on the defense as well.

I expect similarly to kind of how coding is a horizontal across every organization. I think you’ll definitely see cyber being another horizontal that is going to drive a lot of demand, and then I do think you know you’re starting to see other areas, whether it’s mathematical problems, which obviously can then translate into things like forecasting or financial services or supply chain or other workloads.

We’ve seen tremendous amount of adoption of AI in healthcare, both in terms of clinical documentation when doctors talk to patients, but also things like radiology. We’re starting to see it being used more heavily in pharmaceutical research and drug discovery.

We’re seeing it used more and more in the creative space. Whether you know, including for videos and music and things like that. So, I do think you’re going to continue to see both what I call like horizontal use cases, like coding, like cyber, that every organization adopts and then I think you’ll see more vertical scenarios that are industry specific that’ll become standard as well.

As these models get richer, and as with agents, you can just give it a task and it goes off and works and a few hours later, you get a polished, finished, high quality response.

You will find that the demand keeps increasing because as long as there’s a good return, as long as you get more than a dollar’s worth of value out of putting a dollar into the system.

Tae: How do you think the personal and enterprise digital agents OpenClaw, Muse and now Microsoft Autopilot will ramp? What is the potential?

I do think it’ll take off. The trick will be what’s the use case that delivers a business return. AI is expensive, it’s not free.

Different businesses gravitate towards the use cases that help them automate and do things. For example, we’re using it in a variety of internal workloads.

Where historically we would have to wait on someone in the organization to do something and either we didn’t fix things, we weren’t able to take advantage of an opportunity as fast. To the extent that we can have an immediate response, and it’s a really good response, that makes us provide better services and ultimately get more revenue for the business.

I think you’re going to find that organizations increasingly adopt more of those types of use cases, and they’ll gravitate towards the use cases that give them the most differentiation or the most return.

And again, I think coding is a good example where people are doing it today. And I think cyber is a good example where most large organizations are now using these models to look for cyber vulnerabilities in their estate before an attacker finds them.

If you can fix the vulnerability before a bad adversary exploits it, you know that saves you like a thousand to one return versus having an attacker point out the problem for you in a cyber incident.

There’s good examples where we’re seeing these this type of productivity and this type of win. And I think you’re only going to continue with things like Autopilot and the OpenClaw like scenarios.

Those are all examples. I think of the technologies that enable these next generation use cases. Where the ROI is even more significant than a traditional chat scenario.

Tae: How does Microsoft think through when you’re selling Azure AI services, using OpenAI versus Anthropic versus internal? How is that decision made for each customer?

In some cases, customers have specific asks in mind or specific use case, and one model is better than the other. I think also you’re seeing this is a dynamic space.

And if you go back over the last 12 months, I think the world thought that OpenAI was the best model out there. I think if you looked in November [of 2025], December, a lot of people say, Hey, Gemini looks like it maybe is now the best model and lapped OpenAI.

Fast forward to March, people are like, no, no, Anthropic’s the best model.

And I think if you look in the last six weeks, people are saying, hey, [OpenAI] Astra and GPT 6.1 seems like a really good model, and maybe that’s now the best again.

So you’re definitely seeing, at any point in time, in a twelve month period, who has the best model is fairly dynamic more so than any, almost anything I’ve seen in tech in the last twenty or thirty years. Who’s in first, second, and third is just adjusting very, very quickly.

So I always tell customers and partners the nice thing about Microsoft is we’re betting on all of them, and so when you buy Copilot, you can use OpenAI, Anthropic, and our own first-party models. And I think you should expect that the market is going to remain dynamic on the frontier, and what is best for what task is probably going to be somewhat dynamic. And by betting on a harness that’s open and betting on a multi-model solution you can take advantage of whatever the best model is out there.

Then also I think the thing that you’re seeing in particular the last few months is there’s a real price war going on where model costs are coming down, and so again to the extent that you have that flexibility to be able to use multiple models like you do with Copilot and with Microsoft solutions, you benefit from that price war versus if you’re locked into a specific tool or locked into a specific model. You might still benefit from some price wars, but not as directly as if you have switching ability.

And you know we have ability to do auto, and we pick the model for you, and you have the ability to pick the specific model. And we think of that as a feature and a capability. Then with our own Microsoft AI models, we’re going to go after these use cases where we think we can provide even more differentiation from a cost perspective.

And then tying it back to Maia, Maia supports all the models. It’s another example where we’re looking to the price curve and deliver the best AI in an open way that’s multi-model with the best TCO.

text:
OpenAI announced 200 new jobs in Dublin on Monday, adding a new Applied AI Lab at its European Union headquarters and pushing its total hiring commitment in Ireland to at least 450 roles, according to Techcentral.ie.

The announcement brings together the new 200 positions with the 250 roles the company disclosed in July 2026, the company said. OpenAI currently employs over 120 people in Ireland.

The Applied AI Lab will draw on forward deployed engineers who help customers develop and roll out AI applications, along with solutions engineers and privacy engineers. Rounding out the hiring plan are positions across sales and user operations, the company said.

OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar, Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin, and IDA Ireland CEO Michael Lohan gathered on Monday to mark the investment. The new roles will be based at the company's E.U. headquarters at Tropical Fruit Warehouse, which OpenAI plans to occupy from December 2026, the company said.

"Since we opened our E.U. headquarters in Dublin three years ago, Ireland has been critical to our success in Europe," Friar said in a statement. "Through our new Applied AI Lab, expansion of our partnership with Dogpatch Labs and wider roll-out of the SME Academy, we want to help Irish businesses grow, support founders in turning ideas into thriving companies and equip more people across the country to benefit from AI."

Lohan said in a statement that the investment reflects "the strength of Ireland's technical talent and business environment."

As part of the announcement, OpenAI said it will extend its OpenAI for Ireland program for startups, small businesses, and developers. Through a new Founder Cafe initiative with Dogpatch Labs, roughly 150 Irish founders will gain hands-on instruction in ChatGPT, Codex, and API tools, the company said.

The announcement comes as OpenAI has been building out its European leadership. OpenAI appointed Ismail Elmas as vice president of sales for Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, its second senior sales hire from SpaceX's Cursor unit since September. The appointments reflect OpenAI's push for deeper corporate revenue in a region where policymakers have grown wary of reliance on U.S.-built technology.

text:
Dive Brief:

Stryker said Monday it has partnered with soft tissue robotics firm CMR Surgical, investing about $400 million into the company and becoming the exclusive U.S. distributor of CMR’s system.

Cambridge, England-based CMR received Food and Drug Administration clearance for its latest robotic system last year to perform gallbladder procedures in the U.S. As of early 2026, the company had performed more than 45,000 procedures globally, J.P. Morgan analyst Robbie Marcus wrote in a research note.

Stryker had been expected to enter the soft tissue robotics market for years, Stifel analyst Rick Wise wrote in a research note. With competitors Johnson & Johnson and Medtronic receiving FDA nods for their own robots in the U.S., Wise added, “it feels like a now or never moment for Stryker to make the decision.”

Dive Insight:

Competition in robotic surgery is heating up as J&J and Medtronic take on market leader Intuitive. Now, Stryker is entering the foray through its agreement with CMR.

Stryker has a history in robotics with its Mako orthopedic system, reporting record installations in the first quarter.

Given Stryker’s experience with Mako and their large hospital operating room equipment franchise, “the door always seemed open” for Stryker to enter the soft tissue robotic surgery market, Wise wrote.

CMR is roughly second or third in terms of the global robotic installed base, Wise estimated. The company’s robot, called Versius, has a modular design, so it can be moved between operating rooms. While CMR is only authorized for gallbladder procedures in the U.S., the company plans to seek additional soft tissue indications in the future.

The agreement with CMR would give Stryker the exclusive option to buy the robotics company’s remaining shares. Stryker has sales rights for Versius in the U.S., while CMR will continue to lead commercial efforts in other markets.

Andy Pierce, Stryker’s group president for Medsurg and Neurotechnology, said Stryker has evaluated soft tissue robotics for years, and the company chose CMR Surgical “because of the opportunity to help healthcare providers grow robotic-assisted surgery adoption across a broad range of procedures in hospitals and [ambulatory surgery centers].”

J.P. Morgan’s Marcus said Stryker may start with marketing the Versius robot in lower cost facilities, such as ASCs, rather than going head to head with Intuitive’s market leading da Vinci system in hospitals. Marcus doesn’t expect the new partnership to affect Intuitive much, but it could pose a greater threat to other companies that are looking to take a piece of the soft tissue robotics market.

text:
S&P Global Ratings raised Macy’s Inc.’s debt ratings outlook as the retailer has delivered five quarters of positive comparable-store sales alongside stable gross margin. The ratings agency said Macy’s has benefited from a “strategy of adding affordable luxury and luxury brands to attract higher income consumers.”

S&P noted that the performance at its luxury banner Bloomingdale’s has been better than expected, but it remains a small part of the overall business.

S&P said Macy’s credit metrics have remained consistent, including S&P Global Ratings-adjusted debt to EBITDA in the 2x-2.5x range, despite ongoing store closures. As a result of Macy’s improved performance, S&P revised its outlook to positive from stable and affirmed all of its ratings, including ‘BB+’ issuer credit rating. The company’s short-term issuer and commercial paper ratings remain ‘B’.

The positive outlook reflects the possibility of a higher (investment grade) rating over the next 12-18 months if the company continues to demonstrate a track-record of operating performance improvements while maintaining its existing financial policy, including leverage near 2x.

S&P said in its analysis, “We forecast Macy’s Inc. will maintain a solid credit profile, characterized by healthy free operating cash flow (FOCF) generation and disciplined capital allocation. Macy’s has managed S&P adjusted leverage in the 2x-2.5x range post-pandemic when performance has been mixed and includes years of revenue decline and EBITDA contraction as the company closed locations and reinvested in its go-forward store fleet. Macy’s is investing $820 million-$850 million in capital expenditures (capex) annually for store improvements and refurbishments and technology advancements. This level of expenditure supports its strategy to improve the in-store experience and omni-channel capabilities, including artificial intelligence to assist customers shopping online.

“We forecast the company to generate $675 million of FOCF in fiscal 2026 and a more normalized $450 million in 2027. This will support dividends of $205 million and a minimum of $200 million in share repurchases in 2026. In 2027, we forecast dividends to increase to $214 million and for share repurchase capacity to increase to at least $350 million. Cash flow will also benefit from estimated $130 million in asset sale proceeds from closed owned locations. We forecast over $1 billion in balance-sheet cash and a demonstrated track-record of modest share repurchases will lead to leverage in the high-1x.

“Recent financial performance and comparable sales trends suggest Macy’s operational improvements are sustainable, despite ongoing store closures. Macy’s successful execution of the “Bold New Chapter” strategy is supporting its operating performance, including comparable same-store sales growth and gross margin stability. We anticipate the continued expansion of the Bloomingdale’s and Bluemercury banners, combined with a higher-income consumer at Macy’s, could somewhat mitigate the cyclical risks associated with the middle-income exposed Macy’s banner, which exhibits higher price elasticity of demand.

“The Macy’s brand continues to also serve the value-conscious, middle-income shopper. However, it has successfully integrated on-trend, higher-price-point brands such as Good American and Polo Women’s to elevate its assortment and illustrate restored confidence from brand partners. Simultaneously, Bloomingdale’s has capitalized on shifts in the luxury landscape, particularly following the bankruptcy filing of Saks Global, to secure premium brand partnerships including Christian Louboutin and new and on-trend brands such as Skims and Vuori. However, the company’s product offerings under all banners remain discretionary. While the company has been successful in its strategy over the last 12-18 months and the consumer has remained resilient despite weak macroeconomic indicators, the model has not fully been tested in an economic downturn.

“Macy’s comparable owned-plus-licensed-plus-marketplace sales increased 2.7 percent in the second quarter of 2026, the fifth consecutive quarter of growth. Sales momentum was largely propelled by Bloomingdale’s, which delivered 11.3 percent comparable sales growth, underscoring the success of its premium merchandise strategy. Furthermore, the Macy’s banner’s go-forward comparable sales grew 1.1 percent, an improvement from the 0.6 percent growth recorded in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025. We attribute this to inventory management, limiting the need for heavy markdowns and new brands wins leading to a higher average unit retail (AUR) and larger basket sizes. Therefore, we forecast a modest revenue increase for the company (previously a decline) of approximately 0.8 percent for fiscal year 2026 and 0.7 percent for 2027 as low-single-digit comparable sales growth offsets the impact of planned store closures.

“Despite revenue growth improvements, profitability growth will be minimal. We forecast improvements in gross margins in 2026 to 41.2 percent from 40.3 percent as the company receives tariff refunds and negotiated its supply chain costs with key partners. We forecast another modest improvement to 41.8 percent in 2027 due to lower tariffs and better mix. These improvements will not result in meaningful improvements in EBITDA due to SGA growth to support the labor required to operate the stores at the level its strategy calls for. Its 9 percent S&P adjusted EBITDA margin is comparable to other department store peers, but weaker than specialty retailers that operate in a mid-to-high-teen level EBITDA margin. Store closures are no longer a meaningful drag to the EBITDA line and not a component on delaying its improvement. However, we believe achieving SGA leverage over a smaller store base will take time and we do not forecast meaningful EBITDA margin improvement until after 2028.

“Store closures will continue but we expect sustained organic growth in its remaining stores. We believe Macy’s Inc.’s disciplined approach to its physical footprint will enhance liquidity and optimize the long-term profitability of its remaining locations. We expect the company to close approximately 40 total locations in fiscal 2026, following a series of closures in 2024 and 2025. In 2026, we expect the company to exit 31 Macy’s banner locations with the goal of reaching a streamlined, healthy fleet of approximately 350 stores, as the company seeks to exit underperforming mall locations. According to the company, its remaining locations are in A- and B-level malls—which benefit from steadier foot traffic and enhanced service or entertainment tenants. We believe the increased productivity of the remaining “reimagine” stores will offset the reduced store base. Excluding the volatility of the pandemic, revenue per store has remained relatively stable, suggesting its strategic pruning of its store fleet has been successful.

“We forecast low-single-digit organic comparable same-store sales growth. Therefore, we view the lower store count as a manageable strategic realignment toward high-quality, high-traffic environments that support the company’s elevated brand positioning.

“Macy’s continues to invest in its digital ecosystem, including enhancements to its third-party marketplace, AI-driven personalization, and localized fulfillment capabilities. During this digital transformation, its S&P Global Ratings-adjusted EBITDA margins have declined to 9 percent-10 percent from a 14 percent peak, but note not all investments are on the digital side of the business. Macy’s digital sales surged to a pandemic-induced peak of 44 percent from 22 percent in 2018, and the sales mix has stabilized in the low- to mid-30 percent range. We do not anticipate a significant shift in this mix in the near term, as the company has successfully adopted an agnostic approach to consumer purchasing channels. Omni-channel stability allows Macy’s to capture value regardless of whether a transaction occurs in a physical storefront or via a digital interface. As a result, we view the company’s current scale and mix as more efficient and better aligned with modern consumer habits than in previous cycles.

“Macy’s substantial scale and geographic reach maintain its leading market position in the U.S. department store sector. We now assess Macy’s management and governance (M&G) score as neutral. We believe the prior disclosure of a material weakness in its internal control over financial reporting, in which an employee concealed around $151 million in small package delivery expenses over nearly three years, is no longer a concern. Macy’s stated the errors did not materially affect its results of operations or financial position for any historical annual or interim period. The company said this did not affect cash and vendor payments. It determined the matter did not require it to reissue historical financial statements.

“The positive outlook reflects the possibility that we could raise the ratings to investment grade over the next 12-18 months if the company continues to demonstrate a track-record of operating performance improvement while maintaining its existing financial policy including leverage near 2x.”

Dive Brief:

Kroger’s planned acquisition of Giant Eagle could increase concentration in the grocery industry and harm consumers, Sen. Elizabeth Warren wrote in an Oct. 5 letter to the Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Justice.

The $1.65 billion deal, which the grocers announced this summer, is one of three major proposed acquisitions in the food industry that would each “raise competition concerns,” Warren claimed.

Together, the mergers “appear to reveal a growing consolidation trend, driven by weak antitrust enforcement under President Trump, that raises costs and hurts consumers, restaurants, and small businesses,” Warren wrote, asking the agencies to “carefully scrutinize the potential anticompetitive implications under the three pending transactions.”

Dive Insight:

Warren’s letter to the two regulatory bodies that assess the antitrust implications of proposed M&A comes as the grocery industry continues to grapple with ongoing concerns over grocery affordability.

“[F]amilies are paying higher prices for food and groceries while dominant food industry conglomerates continue to rake in sky-high profits,” Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, wrote in the letter.

Kroger’s plan to buy Giant Eagle as well as Sysco’s proposed acquisition of Restaurant Depot, and McCormick’s planned purchase of Unilever’s food business could further consolidate the food and grocery markets, leading to increased prices for consumers, store closures and lost jobs, Warren wrote.

Warren raised concerns that the large store footprint of Kroger, as well as its overlapping presence with Giant Eagle in several markets, could lead to reduced competition in certain areas.

While Kroger’s plan to merge with rival Albertsons was struck down by a federal and a state court, Kroger’s plan to buy Giant Eagle appears poised for a smoother regulatory review, in part due to the tightened scale of this deal, antitrust lawyers told Grocery Dive.

Kroger has said it plans to divest an unspecified number of stores in its bid to win regulatory approval for the Giant Eagle deal. Warren pointed to the divestiture debacle tied to Albertsons’ purchase of Safeway in 2015 as well as the closure of nearly 20% of the stores divested in the 2016 merger of Ahold and Delhaize.

If Kroger provides a robust store divestiture plan in markets where it overlaps with Giant Eagle, the grocers likely have a solid chance of alleviating regulatory concerns, Spencer Waller, a professor at Loyola University Chicago School of Law who specializes in antitrust law, told Grocery Dive earlier this year.
